newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Buba confirms rates to stay unchanged.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buba confirms rates to stay unchanged.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Thursday held its three key interest rates unchanged, delivering formal confirmation that it saw no need to adjust monetary policy at the moment.
"The Bundesbank confirmed its pre-announced statement," said Stephan Schneider, senior Germany economist at Banque Paribas in Frankfurt after the news hit traders' screens.

The central bank said the discount rate remains at 2.50 percent and the Lombard rate remains at the 4.50 percent while the main money market rate, the repo, will stay fixed at three percent for the next two weeks.

Only one day earlier, Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing had primed markets for Thursday's decision with an usually frank comment that another rate cut was "neither to be expected nor necessary".

While Issing's remarks sent the German bond and stock markets sharply lower on Wednesday, independent economists said the comments merely stated the obvious: there are currently no facts that would support another rate cut.

Germany's economic recovery is progressing satisfactorily and more favourable currency rates, especially a slightly firmer dollar, were doing more to nurture growth than another interest rate adjustment could.
Similarly inflation still remains under control, even though higher oil prices were beginning to filter through as seen in a spate of initial October state inflation data.

West German preliminary inflation data reported after the Bundesbank announcement showed a slight increase, measuring unchanged on the month but rising 1.5 percent on the year, after rising 1.4 percent on the year in September.
"We have seen the lows on inflation rates and rates will climb again very, very slowly but that is nothing worrying," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer.

Even as the headline inflation rate is expected to rise slightly early next year as higher prices for some public services impact the data, economists said the Bundesbank would not rush to raise rates on that news.
And while the Bundesbank may wish to see lower capital market rates, independent economists said there is very little guarantee that another small interest rate cut could impact the bond markets.
"The Bundesbank takes it as a given that they can't affect the long end of the market," so there is no need to adjust rates to do so, Paribas' Schneider said.

At the same time the Bundesbank's direct statement on interest rates may be seen to further underscore a policy of not taking extra steps to help certain nations prepare to enter Europe's planned currency union, economists said.
"Issing's comments could be seen to say Germany will not make it easier for Italy to enter the EMU," Baer's Grebe said.
But at the moment Germany's help, in the form of another rate cut, may not even be necessary as was proven in part when Italy on Wednesday cut its discount rate to 7.5 percent, economists added.
Looking further ahead, bond market analysts said that interest cut hopes for Germany appear to have been eliminated for the forseeable future.

"Issing in no way tried to soften his words by adding, as other council members have done, a statement to the effect that one can never say for sure that there will not be another rate cut, and that wipe out all rate cut hopes for the weeks to come," said Irgeen Rust, economist at WestLB in Duesseldorf.
